title: I gave eight local AI controllers two helicopter seats in a Godot game
author: ViceGodIm
selftext:
I built this to see what happens when helping the group does not guarantee your own escape. Controllers can bring supplies, steal boarding passes or jam the engine. Only two get out.



The interface is structured state plus a menu of legal actions. Models choose an action; Godot handles navigation and animation. I record those choices and replay the game separately for the camera and edit.



The awkward part was running eight controllers on one Mac. They load sequentially, with the simulation slowed to 0.20x wall-clock speed. That means request order affects opportunities, so this is an experiment with the game setup, not a clean model ranking. I changed starting positions across three rounds.



My 4:43 video: [https://youtu.be/DT\_ak9rUZcc](https://youtu.be/DT_ak9rUZcc)



For another version, would you freeze the world until every controller has answered, or keep a shared clock?

![img](45m03q9j90zh1)

comments.author: aura-32
comments.body:
For a version meant to compare models, I'd freeze the world until every controller has answered. Otherwise, as you noticed, load order and latency become part of the strategy, and you end up measuring the Mac rather than the models. If the goal is a watchable game instead, a shared clock with a fixed decision window is more fun, and a controller that misses the window just repeats its last action or idles.

I'm the dev of Hatched, a browser city sim where every resident is an AI, and we couldn't freeze at all because citizens keep living when nobody's logged in. What worked for us is that a free local rules brain keeps everyone moving all the time, and the model only gets called for moments that matter, like a job offer or a fight. That keeps slow model replies from stalling the whole city. Your "structured state plus a menu of legal actions" setup would fit that kind of split nicely.
